source_text: Itaque nos hoc prius affirmare debemus quod occulte subrui periclitatur, quantum ualeat apud deum inanitas ista, et ante omnia, unde ratio ipsa processerit hoc modo promerendi deum. tunc enim agnoscetur obseruationis necessitas, cum eluxerit rationis auctoritas a primordio recensendae. acceperat Adam a deo legem non gustandi de arbore agnitionis boni et mali, moriturus si gustasset. uerum et ipse tunc in psychicum reuersus post ecstasin spiritalem, in qua magnum illud sacramentum in Christum et ecclesiam prophetauerat, nec iam capiens quae erant spiritus, facilius uentri quam deo cessit, pabulo potius quam praecepto annuit, salutem gula uendidit. manducauit denique et periit, saluus alioquin, si uni arbusculae ieiunare maluisset; ut iam hinc animalis fides semen suum recognoscat exinde deducens carnalium adpetitionem et spiritalium recusationem. teneo igitur a primordio homicidam gulam tormentis atque suppliciis inediae puniendam, etiamsi deus nulla ieiunia praecepisset. ostendens tamen, unde sit occisus Adam, mihi reliquerat intellegenda remedia offensae, qui offensam demonstrarat. ultro cibum, quibus modis quibusque temporibus potuissem, pro ueneno deputarem et antidotum famem sumerem, per quam purgarem mortis a primordio causam in me quoque cum ipso genere transductam, certus hoc deum uelle cuius contrarium noluit satisque confidens placituram illi continentiae curam, a quo damnatam comperissem incontinentiae culpam. porro, cum et ipse ieiunium mandet et animam conquassatam proprie utique cibi angustiis sacrificium appellet, quis iam dubitabit omnium erga uictum macerationum hanc fuisse rationem, qua rursus interdicto cibo et obseruato praecepto primordiale iam delictum expiaretur, ut homo per eandem materiam causae satis deo faciat per quam offenderat id est per cibi interdictionem, atque ita salutem aemulo modo redaccenderet inedia, sicut extinxerat sagina, pro unico inlicito plura licita contemnens?
thought_title: The original sin of eating and fasting as its remedy
orientation: Tertullian is answering the opponents' claim that fasting is unnecessary by going back to God's first command to Adam in Eden.
pass_a_gloss: And so we ought first to affirm this, which is in danger of being secretly undermined: how much this emptiness is worth before God, and before all things, whence the very reason proceeded for meriting God in this way. For then the necessity of the observance will be recognized, when the authority of the reason has shone forth, which must be reviewed from the beginning. Adam had received from God a law of not tasting from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, being about to die if he tasted. But he himself, then turned back into an unspiritual man after the spiritual ecstasy in which he had prophesied that great sacrament concerning Christ and the church, and no longer grasping the things that were of the Spirit, yielded more easily to his belly than to God, nodded to food rather than to the command, sold his salvation for gluttony. He ate, in short, and perished, though otherwise safe if he had preferred to fast from one little tree; so that from this point the unspiritual faith may recognize its own seed, deriving from there the appetite for fleshly things and the refusal of spiritual things. I hold therefore that from the beginning gluttony is a murderer, to be punished with torments and punishments of fasting, even if God had commanded no fasts. Nevertheless, showing whence Adam was slain, he had left for me to understand the remedies of the offense, he who had demonstrated the offense. Of my own accord I would count food, in whatever ways and at whatever times I could, as poison, and I would take hunger as an antidote, through which I would purge the cause of death from the beginning, transmitted into me also along with the race itself, certain that God wills this whose contrary he did not will, and confident enough that the care of self-control would please him, from whom I had learned that the fault of lack of self-control was condemned. Furthermore, since he himself commands fasting and calls a soul crushed, properly indeed by the straits of food, a sacrifice, who will now doubt that this was the reason of all macerations concerning food, by which, with food again forbidden and the command observed, the original sin would now be expiated, so that man through the same material of the cause might make satisfaction to God through which he had offended, that is through the prohibition of food, and so might rekindle salvation by fasting in a rival manner, just as overindulgence had extinguished it, despising many lawful things in place of one unlawful thing?

pass_b_english: So I must first defend what is being quietly undermined: how much this emptiness is worth before God, and above all, where the very logic of earning God's favor in this way came from. For the necessity of the observance will be recognized once the authority of its rationale shines out, and that rationale must be traced from the beginning.

Adam had received from God the law not to taste of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and he would die if he tasted it. But after his spiritual ecstasy, in which he had prophesied that great mystery of Christ and the church, he fell back into a merely unspiritual state. No longer able to grasp the things of the Spirit, he yielded to his belly more easily than to God, nodded to food rather than to the command, and sold his salvation for gluttony. He ate, and he perished, though he would have been safe if he had chosen to fast from one little tree. From this point on, let unspiritual faith recognize its own seed, deriving from there its appetite for fleshly things and its rejection of spiritual things.

I hold, then, that from the very beginning gluttony is a murderer, to be punished with the torments and penalties of hunger, even if God had commanded no fasts. Yet by showing me where Adam was slain, God left me to understand the remedies for the offense, since he had shown me the offense itself. Of my own accord I would count food as poison, in whatever ways and at whatever times I could, and take hunger as an antidote, through which I might purge the cause of death that had been passed down from the beginning into me along with the race itself. I would be certain that God wills this, whose contrary he did not will, and confident enough that the discipline of self-control would please him, since I had learned that the fault of lack of self-control was condemned by him.

Furthermore, since he himself commands fasting and calls a crushed soul, crushed precisely by the straits of food, a sacrifice, who will now doubt that this was the rationale of all mortifications of appetite: that by again forbidding food and observing the command, the original sin might be expiated, so that through the same material of the cause, the prohibition of food, man might make satisfaction to God through the very thing by which he had offended, and so fasting might rekindle salvation, just as overindulgence had extinguished it, by despising many permitted foods in place of the one forbidden one?
